problem: Waypoint-based VLN-CE pipelines (waypoint predictor, navigator, low-level controller) propose isolated node-centric waypoints that often lie in obstacles or unreachable regions. The controller's executed path also deviates from what the navigator planned (planning-control inconsistency).
motivation: Waypoints are the interface between high-level planning and low-level control in VLN-CE, so unreachable or inconsistently executed sub-goals cause collisions and error accumulation over long horizons. Diffusion policies (e.g. NoMaD) can generate collision-free, multi-modal trajectories, which suggests making the executable trajectory itself the candidate unit.
key_idea: Replace node-centric waypoints with executable trajectory candidates generated by a TSDF-guided diffusion policy, and let the navigator plan over these trajectories using their path geometry.
insight: Inference-time TSDF gradient guidance is the largest contributor to reachability: %Open rises from 88.34 to 95.84 (DINOv3) and from 86.87 to 94.96 (ResNet-50). Removing the TWP raises CR from 0.004 to 0.12, and removing TEN lowers SR by 1.0 with CR unchanged. Guidance is a trade-off: SR peaks at 3 guided denoising steps, and more steps over-constrain the diffusion distribution and hurt SR.
method: Trajectory Waypoint Predictor (TWP): a panoramic RGB-D encoder (DINOv3 for RGB, DDPPO ResNet-50 for depth, feature fusion, Transformer panorama encoder) feeds an MLP that predicts a distribution over direction bins x step-count bins. Its top-K outputs form the location priors (K up to 5).

Conditional diffusion policy: for each prior, the condition state is the sector visual feature plus the prior's positional embedding. A DDPM (10 denoising steps) generates a 12-step relative-displacement trajectory per prior.

TSDF cost guidance: a local TSDF map is built from depth. At inference, the gradient of a hinge collision cost is subtracted from the denoised output (weight 0.003, step 1.0). It is applied only in the first 3 denoising iterations.
Adaptive trajectory truncation: each fixed-horizon trajectory is cut to the predicted step count ŝ_k, giving variable-length candidates whose endpoints are the trajectory waypoints.

Visually-grounded trajectory encoding: BEVBert-style metric map features are sampled at each trajectory point and combined with position and step embeddings. A learnable-query attention pools them into an edge feature e_τ.

Trajectory-enhanced topo-metric map: e_τ is added to the ghost-node visual embedding, and a parallel trajectory-to-cell enhancement is applied to the metric map. A dual-branch transformer (GASA + self-attention) scores the candidates, and the agent directly executes the selected trajectory.

Training data: TWP is trained on 120k+ waypoint-trajectory pairs from MP3D + HM3D (794 extra scenes), with expert paths TSDF-refined and stitched. TEN is pretrained on R2R and fine-tuned online with DAgger, following ETPNav.

setting.backbone: DINOv3 + DDPPO ResNet-50 encoders, diffusion policy TWP, and ETPNav/BEVBert-style topo-metric transformer navigator (trained)

results: On R2R-CE val-unseen the method reaches SR 60.3 / SPL 51.4 / OSR 68.1, beating BEVBert (SR 59, SPL 50) and ETPNav (SR 57, SPL 49). On val-seen it reaches SR 68.8 / SPL 60.2. The predictor gets %Open 95.84 against SmartWay's 87.26, and collision rate drops to 0.004 from 0.12 without TWP.
limitations: Gains over the strongest baselines are small (about 1.3 SR and 1.4 SPL on val-unseen), and only R2R-CE is evaluated, with no RxR-CE and no real-robot tests.
TSDF guidance needs careful tuning (3 steps is best) and adds inference cost through 10 diffusion steps per candidate.
The training-data advantage (an extra 794 HM3D scenes) is not separated from the paradigm's contribution in the navigation comparison.
